extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories about illness/death (obituaries, death notices, surgical-case reports) and for reporting political elections (pre-election analysis, election-day coverage, and returns). Aimed at newsroom practice and student instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three common kinds of election stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Three common kinds of election stories are: (1) an analysis of political conditions preceding an election with or without a forecast of the result, (2) a description of election day conditions and events, (3) the results of the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to choose the appropriate approach and structure for an election piece; analysis/forecast pieces emphasize background and likely outcomes, day-of stories emphasize atmosphere and incidents, and returns focus on outcomes and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election return story content
rubrics_metrics.description: Election return stories consist largely of summaries of the most important results of the election, such as: (1) the candidates elected and defeated, (2) the majority or plurality of the successful candidates, (3) the effect of the election on the political complexion of legislative bodies, (4) causes of victory and defeat, (5) statements by candidates and party managers in regard to the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing returns, include these elements as the core facts and explanations; quantify margins and link outcomes to broader political control and causes; include immediate reactions from key actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and separation of news and editorials in political reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some newspapers are sufficiently independent in politics to treat political news without partisan bias, many papers still present such news from the point of view of their editorial policy. There is a growing tendency, however, to present both sides fairly in news columns and to confine partisanship to editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for even-handed presentation in news copy; keep partisan commentary and advocacy in labeled editorial pages rather than in news items. Balance quotes and perspectives when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary: include identity, age, and cause of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Obituaries routinely state the deceased's name, age, and the cause or immediate circumstances of death (e.g., 'died yesterday ... Heart disease is believed to have caused his death', 'The cause of death was pneumonia brought on by exposure').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear factual information on who died, when, and why as the lead elements; corroborate cause-of-death statements with coroner or physician when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary: career history and public/service roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a summary of the deceased's career and public roles (examples include detailed accounts of service in a profession—fire department service, editorial leadership, university deanship—or political prominence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a concise chronological sketch of major positions, achievements, and long-term service that explains why the person is newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary: community contributions and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight contributions to the community and notable acts of charity or public service (e.g., saving 'unknowns' from Potter’s Field, leading charitable initiatives, founding institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples and anecdotes to show impact on community and to give readers a sense of character and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary: family, survivors, and funeral arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include mention of surviving relatives, next of kin, and funeral/memorial arrangements (e.g., 'The funeral will be held tomorrow afternoon ... The burial will be in the Springfield cemetery').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide names and relationships when relevant and known, and state time/place details for services so readers can attend or pay respects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary: humanizing anecdotes and personal detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Use anecdotes, personal habits, sayings, and small incidents to humanize the subject (examples: 'Tse-Ne-Gat made for himself a long whistle... the sight the other sufferers there loved', 'Walter’s last request that No.1 be brought in on time').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select illustrative stories that reveal character, values, or quirks; such details make obituaries engaging and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death/discovery reporting: circumstances and official statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the circumstances of discovery and official findings when relevant (police entry, coroner statements, diary entries indicating illness, timelines such as 'life had been extinct twenty-four hours').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide factual sequence of events and official attributions, avoid speculation, and include documentary evidence when available (diaries, coroner reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical-operation news: case details and professional attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical operation stories describe the patient's background and injury, the date and place of operation, the operating physician, the surgical technique employed, and the outcome (successful, temporary recovery, or death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name hospitals and surgeons, describe the rationale (e.g., brain pressure from skull dent), give follow-up condition and broader medical significance, and include expert commentary on implications for treatment or reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical-operation news: significance for the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should note the broader significance of a procedure (e.g., 'full of significance as to possibilities along these lines', 'opens up a new field in surgery') and mention planned further tests or research (vivisection tests to determine limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place novel or unusual medical cases in context: explain why they matter to medicine or public health and report on proposed next steps or controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying political news: treat routine political events like other news
rubrics_metrics.description: Most political news falls into one of the general classes of stories already considered. Party conventions, campaign meetings, political speeches, interviews with candidates and party managers, for example, are treated like similar material in other fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report political events using the same structural approaches applicable to events, speeches, and interviews in other beats—focus on straightforward reporting, salient facts, and relevant context.
